comments.text: What stood out to me in this documentary is that it looks past the castles and Dracula stories and shows everyday life in Romania, from modern Bucharest, Brașov and Timișoara to the wooden villages of Maramureș and the Danube Delta. The chapter on work and the economy is the part that connects most with anyone thinking about moving there, because it sits alongside homes, food, family life and the real challenges people face. I liked the question it keeps returning to, why so many Romanians stay attached to their homeland despite economic hardship and opportunities abroad, and the answer it finds in family, community and tradition. The contrast between horse-drawn carts in rural valleys and modern city life makes the country feel real rather than postcard-perfect. After watching the work and economy chapter, what surprised you most about how people earn a living in Romania?

comments.text: The Romanian language is difficult for English speakers to learn.  The grammar rules are insane with many exceptions to the rules. It also has borrowed words from slavic that would be unfamiliar to English speakers.  Indiana University used to teach it but dropped it after the professor there retired.  Only a few universities around the US teach it now.
